Changing several of them together could produce movement without showing why it occurred. Before using the simulation to study control of the robot, I needed to check the translated circuits and their mechanical connections separately, then examine the coupled model with controlled changes to its inputs or mechanics.

One gap concerned the mechanical model. The Li walker used simplified biological muscles, whereas this project also required a human musculoskeletal reference and a robot model with BPA routing and force production. A controller that produced motion in one of these models could not be assumed to work in the others. The OpenSim-to-MuJoCo conversion and BPA-force calculation made those comparisons possible. A second gap concerned the controller itself. Transferring a circuit required preserving its connectivity, synaptic strengths, neuron dynamics, and sensory inputs. Agreement in burst timing could otherwise conceal a changed mechanism, such as a rhythm imposed by alternating contact inputs. Matched circuit tests therefore distinguish intrinsic rhythmic activity from sensory-driven alternation. Coupled perturbation tests then ask whether a controller continues to produce supported progression when the mechanics change while its conductances remain fixed.

A third gap was practical: the mechanical and neural models used different construction environments. Scripted MuJoCo and SNS-Toolbox models supported automated evaluations, while the MATLAB mechanical models and CAD-derived mechanisms needed a graphical neural interface. The SNS-Simscape library supplied editable neural and sensory blocks for that workflow. Its verification must address both circuit behavior and exchange of forces and measurements with a mechanical model. Importing a mechanism alone answers neither question. Coupled tests ask how the resulting motion changes with support, sensory pathways, or disturbances. The results below demonstrate each level within a stated scope. They establish a working basis for controlled neuromechanical experiments while identifying the balance, model-transfer, and controller-tuning problems that remain.

Existing tools supply the components of this framework. Simulink supplies graphical circuit assembly, and Simscape Multibody supplies mechanical imports, including CAD-derived mechanisms. AnimatLab contains the original walker and reference circuits. My contribution connects these components through the model conversions, actuator calculations, circuit implementations, and tests described below.

\subsection{Support, Stimulation, and Parameter Search}\label{sec:sns_experiment_controls}

The MuJoCo simulations allow mechanical support to be specified independently of the neural controller. A virtual harness applies forces and torques to the body: it can hold the model above the ground, lower it into contact, retain vertical support, or constrain selected directions of translation and rotation. These settings represent different experimental conditions. Suspended motion tests whether the controller and actuators can move the limbs, whereas supported ground contact adds loading and sensory feedback. Progression with retained support is reported separately from unsupported walking.

The training sequence, or curriculum, progresses from simpler conditions toward greater mechanical demand. Its stages include air stepping, supported standing, ground-contact stepping, and reduced support. Parameters can be held fixed to test transfer between stages or re-tuned at a new stage to seek a viable configuration. These procedures answer different questions: successful re-tuning shows that a configuration can be found, while a fixed-controller test shows whether an existing controller tolerates the change. A stage is demonstrated only when its stated motion and stability criteria are met.

Neural interventions include tonic currents, brief stimuli to selected circuit populations, and removal of specified feedback or coupling pathways. Mechanical interventions include timed forces at the pelvis and changes to segment mass and inertia. The recorded outputs include membrane voltage, actuator force, joint motion, foot contact, body position and orientation, and harness force. Together, these controls allow the neural response and the resulting motion to be examined in the same experiment.

Optuna automates parameter searches within specified bounds. Each candidate is evaluated using measures such as bilateral contact cycles, inter-leg phase, forward displacement, joint trajectories, posture, and survival. The score determines which candidate is selected; a separate replay checks that candidate under the stated conditions. Optuna is used as a search tool, without a claim that it finds a global optimum or outperforms other optimizers. Interpretation depends on the objective and validity checks, including confirmation that every searched parameter reaches the implemented model.

Two-level models separate the timing of the locomotor rhythm from the distribution of activity to muscles. This distinction has been extended to genetically identified interneuron classes \citep{rybak_organization_2015} and circuits controlling muscles that cross two joints \citep{shevtsova_modeling_2016}. The latter problem also arises in a robot: activating a two-joint muscle can affect motion at both joints, so its control cannot be assigned to either joint in isolation.

Coupling the circuit to a musculoskeletal model adds the effects of mechanics and sensory feedback. Such models show how afferent feedback shapes CPG output \citep{markin_afferent_2010} and how body mechanics and feedback influence the behavior of different CPG architectures \citep{deng_biomechanical_2022}. Human locomotion models combine locomotor primitives with Ia, II, and Ib pathways and Renshaw cells to examine their contributions to control \citep{dirusso_investigating_2023}. Other models examine interlimb responses to sudden loss of ground support \citep{shinohara_mechanisms_2025}. Section~\ref{sec:bg_compneuro} describes these circuits, and Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} develops tools for implementing and testing related controllers.

What distinguishes the present program from all three lines is the combination it attempts: an anatomically grounded controller (two-layer CPG with Ia, Ib, II, and contact feedback), a biomechanically validated pneumatic model (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}), and an eventual physical robot.
after: The third line uses biologically grounded synthetic nervous systems with explicit neuron and synapse models \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Their circuit structure allows a researcher to change a specified pathway and examine its effect on behavior. Related work includes motor-module bipedal walkers \citep{ichimura_pathological_2019}, two-layer RG/PF control of a musculoskeletal macaque model \citep{nishizaki_gait_2026}, and two-level CPG control of muscle-driven robotic hind legs \citep{fukuoka_autonomous_2021}.
